articles.title: Ebola: Why is there still no vaccine?
articles.summary: Ebola has been known about for decades, but there is still no vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain of the virus causing the current outbreak. New research raises hopes of protection against the…

image.caption: Researchers are working to develop a vaccine against the strain of Ebola responsible for the current outbreak Image: Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: 1976: A hitherto unknown disease breaks out near the Ebola river in the country then known as Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). This was the first scientifically documented Ebola epidemic.

Now, 50 years on, the DRC once again finds itself at the center of a major Ebola outbreak. This time the pathogen is the less common Bundibugyo type of the genus Orthoebolavirus. The virus was identified in 2007 during an outbreak in Bundibugyo, Uganda. Another outbreak occurred in the DRC in 2012.
Bundibugyo: Preparations could have been made
How can a virus that has been known for decades continue to infect thousands of people, yet there is still no licensed vaccine or official treatment?

Torsten Feldt, a doctor of tropical medicine at Düsseldorf's University Hospital, sees this as a missed opportunity. "We had come across the Bundibugyo virus in two previous outbreaks: 2007 in Uganda and 2012 in DR Congo. So we had enough time to develop vaccines and therapeutic options. But we didn't make use of this opportunity, meaning crucial time was lost during the current outbreak."

Leonie Mayer from the German Center for Infection Research (DZIF) and the Institute for Infection Research and Vaccine Development at the University Medical Center in Hamburg-Eppendorf agrees. "They could of course have developed a vaccine and run pre-clinical trials before," Mayer told DW. She stressed, however, that their effectiveness can only be assessed and confirmed during an actual outbreak.
Mayer is the lead author of a recently published study that examined whether Ervebo, an Ebola vaccine that has already been licensed, can be used against other types of Ebola as well.
Congo's Ebola crisis: Fear, mistrust and a growing outbreak
Why Ebola is a good candidate for vaccine development

From an immunological point of view, and compared to — for example — influenza or HIV, Ebola is a very worthwhile candidate for a vaccine. Influenza viruses are constantly mutating, and the human immunodeficiency virus is particularly good at evading our immune defenses. Ebola is far more predictable.
"I think — and perhaps it's kind of a blessing in disguise — that it will be relatively straightforward to develop a vaccine against Bundibugyo," says Mayer.

Herein lies the paradox. From a scientific point of view, Ebola is a good vaccine candidate, yet there is still no licensed form of prevention against the Bundibugyo variant that is currently circulating.

Mayer explains that vaccines cannot be developed as a precautionary measure against every potential pathogen. Lack of funding or the prioritization of other pathogens often have a role to play. Many researchers had assumed that a fresh outbreak of the Sudan Ebola virus was more likely, and vaccine development for this strain is more advanced.
Different types of Ebola

Another part of the problem is that Ebola is not one single virus. The known, highly dangerous orthoebolaviruses include Ebola virus (EBOV), previously called the Zaire Ebola virus (ZEBOV), the Sudan virus (SUDV), and the Bundibugyo virus (BDBV). The existing vaccine, Ervebo, was developed and licensed for use against the Zaire variant. But there is still no approved protection against the others.
This is why the existing Ebola vaccine has been of only limited use to people in the areas of the current outbreak.

Another factor may also be relevant: The Bundibugyo virus appears to be less aggressive than the Zaire variant. At first, that sounds like good news, but it may make it harder to contain, as people remain mobile for longer after being infected, and can pass on the virus without realizing.
Ervebo vaccine: Immune response to Bundibugyo

In the recently published study, Mayer's research team from the DZIF investigated whether the already licensed Ebola vaccine could trigger an immune response not only against EBOV, but against other types of Ebola as well. They found cross-reactive T-cell responses against Bundibugyo, and also, to a lesser extent, against the Sudan virus.

For Mayer, this is already an important finding: "We now know that the immune cells can most likely also recognize the Bundibugyo virus." But she also observes: "Our data does not enable us to answer the question of whether this immune response actually provides protection, or if it results in a milder progression of the disease." This is currently an important gap in our knowledge.
Why the existing vaccine cannot currently be deployed
If there's a vaccine that has already been licensed, and indications that it could protect people, why isn't it simply being deployed?

Mayer explains the dilemma. For one thing, she says, it's not ethical to deploy a vaccine if you're not sure whether or how well it works. Also, if it were used on a large scale, it would no longer be possible to establish whether it actually works: A reduction in cases could also be a result of other measures, or the epidemic might already have passed its peak.

Jürgen May, a specialist in tropical diseases at the Bernhard Nocht Institute, also warns against mass vaccination: "Mass vaccination without proof of efficacy could create a false sense of security, forfeit trust, and, if it does not provide sufficient protection, make study impossible."

It's very important for there to be acceptance on the ground. "If we inoculate people with a vaccine on a large scale, and afterwards it turns out that it was nothing like as effective as we expected, it's very difficult to communicate that to people on the ground," Mayer says. In a worst-case scenario, people could subsequently refuse inoculation with more effective vaccines.
Why Ebola is still so difficult to contain

But the current outbreak also shows that medical innovation alone is not enough. Conflicts, difficult transport routes, attacks on healthcare facilities, and gaps in contact tracing all make it harder to contain.

blocks.caption: The DRC has had more than 10,000 cases of Bundibugyo since May. Recently, it has also been reported in Kenya and NigeriaImage: Andrew Kasuku/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Torsten Feldt says identifying Bundibugyo is no longer a problem in itself. What is often limiting is the practical availability of diagnostic tools. "In remote or conflict-affected regions, samples often have to be transported over long distances," he explains.

Here we see another Ebola paradox. The world is getting ever better at diagnosing infections, but it still struggles to contain outbreaks fast enough. The authors of an article in the current issue of Nature come to the same conclusion: The problem is often not identifying cases, but the speed with which people react. Finding Ebola is often easier now than stopping Ebola, they write.
From a Bundibugyo vaccine to a pan-Ebola one?

Many researchers believe the current crisis could potentially also provide a great opportunity. The so-called Tumaini study, which is testing different vaccine candidates, has now been launched in the DRC.
These include Ervebo, developed by Oxford University, and a Moderna mRNA vaccine. The study aims to provide the first reliable data about their efficacy against the Bundibugyo virus.

Whether these vaccines could still help control the current outbreak is uncertain. There is hope, but experts estimate that, realistically, it will be several months before any such vaccine is available for widespread use; perhaps not until mid-2027.

"Ideally, we will develop cross-reactive pan-Ebola vaccines," Christof Geldmacher, a co-author of the DZIF study, says of their long-term plans. This is also something that is being worked on. For now, though, the focus is on developing an effective vaccine against the Bundibugyo variant of the virus.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: Richard Lloyd, founding member and guitarist of punk band Television, dies aged 75
articles.summary:
Known for sophisticated musical style in band that played significant role in emerging 1970s punk rock movement

Richard Lloyd, known for his sophisticated musical style as a founding member…

blocks.text: Richard Lloyd, known for his sophisticated musical style as a founding member and guitarist for the influential punk band Television, has died at the age of 75.

His family confirmed that Lloyd died Saturday morning at his home in Chattanooga, Tennessee. “His loving wife Sheila and his dog Willie Mays were with him at the end,” his family said in a statement to Rolling Stone.
According to his family, Lloyd’s death was caused by cholangiocarcinoma, a form of bile duct cancer that he was diagnosed with in March 2026.
A crowdfunding campaign had revealed that Lloyd had developed tumors in his liver and, crucially, there was one that could not be surgically removed.

Television, which formed in 1973, played a significant role in the emerging punk rock movement that grew up around CBGB, the legendary former music venue on the Bowery in New York City. The group was among the earliest punk acts to perform at the downtown venue, which had previously focused mainly on country and bluegrass music.

During a 2007 interview, Lloyd reflected on his role in shaping the club’s history, declaring: “CBGB’s is the most famous rock ‘n’ roll club to have ever existed and I fucking created it! I was the invisible force behind it.”

Television recorded just two studio albums during its peak in the late 1970s. The band’s first album, released in 1977, was Marquee Moon, which has since earned widespread recognition as a landmark recording. Rolling Stone ranked it No 107 on its 2023 list of the 500 greatest albums of all time. The record is still considered one of the most influential guitar-driven albums in rock history.

In a 2005 review, the Guardian described his performance, writing that “Lloyd’s guitar was the louder in a lopsided sound mix, so it was impossible to overlook the amount of ground he was covering. Crisp, crunchy chords, dextrous fills and torrential Van Halen-style solos tumbled from his fingers.”

articles.title: FAA announces first US digital air traffic control towers in Florida and Alaska
articles.summary:
Systems provide 360-degree view of airport operations, but concerns have been raised about the technology

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has announced that the first digital air…

blocks.text: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has announced that the first digital air traffic control towers in the US are officially operational, bringing new technology first to smaller airports in Florida and Alaska as the Trump administration presses ahead with updating the country’s ageing aviation infrastructure.

The systems are now online at the Bartow executive airport (KBOW) in Florida and the Kenai municipal airport (PAEN) in Alaska, with five additional regional airports slated to receive the technology next.

The digital towers use advanced camera systems and digital displays to give air traffic controllers a continuous, 360-degree view of airport operations, including runways, taxiways and surrounding airspace, according to the agency.

The FAA maintains that the technology is not intended to replace human controllers. Instead, the systems are designed to provide greater visibility and additional information to help controllers perform their existing duties.

“Our air traffic controllers continue to do the critical job of keeping aircraft safely separated, and we’re giving them better technology to do that,” said the FAA’s administrator, Bryan Bedford, in a statement.
“Digital towers provide controllers with greater visibility of airport activity and more information to make critical decisions,” he added.

Bedford is scheduled to appear before the House transportation and infrastructure committee next week, where he will face questions about the progress and challenges surrounding the administration’s ongoing $12.5bn modernization initiative.
The effort aims to replace decades-old equipment still used throughout the aviation system, including copper telecommunications lines, floppy disks and paper strips used to track aircraft.

Congress approved $12.5bn over five years in June 2025 to support air traffic control reforms, but the Trump administration is seeking another $30bn from the legislative branch to fund additional improvements.

Concerns about the types of technology being implemented within air traffic control have been gaining traction alongside the increasing unease about artificial intelligence as a whole. In September, the FAA rolled out a new AI software tool called the Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (Smart).
Trump has been heavily criticized for his response to a national shortage of air traffic controllers following last year’s government shutdown.

Staffing levels in control towers and many related aspects of US air traffic safety systems have been under especially close scrutiny since a midair collision between a passenger jet and a military helicopter on the outskirts of Washington DC in 2025 that killed 67 people. It was the deadliest crash in the US for more than 20 years and the authorities later deemed it “100% preventable”.

articles.title: 'Absolutely' possible: Vancouver, Victoria mayors back Ottawa's bid to end homelessness
articles.summary: The federal Liberal budget, delivered on Thursday, has set aside $11.2 billion over the next four years in a bid to end homelessness in the next 10 years.

image.caption: Possessions belonging to people experiencing homelessness on the 900-block of Pandora Avenue in Victoria, B.C. on Dec. 16, 2025. The federal government has announced new funding with a goal to end homelessness within 10 years. (Kathryn Marlow/CBC )

blocks.text: British Columbia·New
The federal Liberal budget, delivered on Thursday, has set aside $11.2 billion over the next four years in a bid to end homelessness in the next 10 years.
Federal Housing Minister Gregor Robertson made a similar pledge while mayor of Vancouver
The federal government is taking a big swing with a promise that might sound familiar to Vancouverites.
The Liberal budget, delivered on Thursday, has set aside $11.2 billion over the next four years in a bid to end homelessness in the next 10 years.
It's an echo of the promise then Vancouver mayor Gregor Robertson made in 2008 — and was ultimately unable to fulfil.
Is Ottawa's promise to end homelessness within 10 years possible?
Speaking in Winnipeg on Friday, Robertson, now federal housing minister, said he didn't have the right tools at the time.
"We did not have the support," Robertson said.
"As a city, we set the goal — the federal and provincial governments were not co-ordinating, were not investing in the scale that was needed to solve the challenge in Vancouver."
As housing minister, Robertson is now driving the bus, and he says the federal government is on board.

Ottawa's plan targets homelessness prevention, expanding access to housing and funding new mental health infrastructure. Components include more support for unhoused veterans, helping low-income people cover rent and building new mental health and addiction treatment facilities.

Metro Vancouver's 2025 Point-in-Time Homeless Count estimated the region's population of unhoused people at more than 5,200. The city's own homeless count found more than 2,700 of them were in Vancouver itself.
Newly-elected Vancouver Mayor Pete Fry says he will reverse the previous council's freeze on new supportive housing in the city. (CBC)
Newly-minted Vancouver Mayor Pete Fry says he's already been in conversation with Robertson, and that the pledge is "aspirational, but very possible."
"The reality is, it requires investment in housing and shelters for folks who are unhoused and triage and supportive housing and all the things that seem to be commitments in this budget," Fry said.
He said it will require close partnerships between Ottawa, the provincial government and the city.
A key step in that, he said, will be reversing former mayor Ken Sim's freeze on supportive housing in the city.
Homelessness has also become a flashpoint in British Columbia's capital.
Newly re-elected Mayor Marianne Alto agreed the goal "absolutely is" possible — provided that senior levels of government cooperate with municipalities and provide enough resources.
Victoria Mayor Marianne Alto speaks at a July 2, 2025, news conference. Alto says she hopes her city's existing homelessness programs can be integrated with new federal funding. (Mike McArthur/CBC)

Alto pointed to Victoria's Community Safety and Wellbeing Plan, as a model. The program aims to transition people off the streets, through shelters and supportive housing and into independent housing.
"That's the type of program that we hope will be included in this federal funding and with the support of the province," she said.
"And if that's the case, then we know that there will be success because we've already proven it."
Alto said the city needs hundreds more supportive and below market units, which will require senior government funding.
Back in Vancouver, the head of one of the region's busiest homelessness and outreach service providers said he was feeling "hopeful" about the announcement.
United Gospel Mission president Dean Kurpjuweit said Ottawa's pledge sets out a clear timeline without attaching some of the strings that came with previous promises of capital funding.

But he said once that funding is used to build units, it will need to be matched by operating funds from the provincial government to provide ongoing care and support services for the people they house.
LISTEN | Ottawa pledges to end homelessness in 10 years:
On The Coast13:10Ottawa pledges $11.2B over the next four years to end homelessness within 10 years
"Probably my biggest fear is that the provincial dollars either won't come or the provincial dollars won't come adequately," he said.
"Or, you know, they come, but they only come for a period of time and once that period of time is over, that's the end of it."
B.C.'s new Conservative government has yet to be sworn in, and incoming premier Lorne Doerkson did not address the homelessness pledge in his response to the federal budget this week.
All eyes will now be on the new government's first provincial budget, to see if its strategy to address homelessness lines up with Ottawa's.
With files from Katie DeRosa

articles.title: Israeli president tasks Gadi Eisenkot with forming government
articles.summary: President Isaac Herzog has picked former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, leader of an anti-Netanyahu alliance, to take the first shot at trying to form a government, with tricky coalition talks…

image.caption: Gadi Eisenkot leads a broad coalition of parties aligned against current leader Benjamin Netanyahu Image: Shir Torem/REUTERS

blocks.text: Israeli President Isaac Herzog has chosen Gadi Eisenkot to have the first opportunity to form a new Israeli government, according to a statement released by his office on Saturday evening.

The statement said Eisenkot was informed of Herzog's "intention to task him with forming a government" and would be invited to the president's residence, where a formal ceremony will take place on Sunday.
The decision comes after a neck-and-neck race with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel's October election.

Eisenkot's wide-ranging group, fashioned in opposition to Netanyahu, won 48 of the Israeli parliament's 120 seats in October's elections. Netanyahu's camp secured 53, leaving neither with the required majority of 61 seats.
Former Israeli military chief Eisenkot is the leader of the centrist Yashar party and heads an anti-Netanyahu alliance.
While Netanyahu ruled out working with Arab parties to gain a majority, both Arab majority lists had announced during the week that they would recommend Eisenkot to be next prime minister.
Can Netanyahu survive his last big fight?
What happens next?
The move is the first step toward what will almost certainly be complicated coalition talks.

Should Eisenkot succeed in forming a government, he would take over as prime minister from Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving premier, whose religious-nationalist coalition lost its majority in the election, despite emerging as the largest bloc.
Although Eisenkot was runner up, he managed to secure endorsements from leaders of Arab parties, which are opposed to Netanyahu.
Eisenkot faces a tricky path to forming a government, involving difficult constellations of Arab and ultra-Orthodox parties. He will have 28 days to round up the 61 votes needed to form a government.
Herzog can provide a 14-day extension if Eisenkot comes up short before the mandate must be offered to someone else.
If no candidate succeeds, Israel will head to fresh elections.
Could Arab voters hold the key in Israel's election?

articles.summary:
Knesset has been deadlocked since election last month when Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition lost its majority

Israel’s president has ⁠chosen Gadi Eisenkot, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s…

articles.title: Trump offers White House press secretary role to Dana White
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has offered the job of White House press secretary to Dana White, the chief executive of the Ultimate Fighting Championship.

image.caption: President Donald Trump and UFC CEO Dana White arrive for the "UFC Freedom 250" mixed martial arts event on the South Lawn of the White House on June 14. Image: Kent Nishimura/AFP

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump announced on Saturday that he has asked Dana White, the CEO of Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC), to serve as White House press secretary.
"I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States," Trump wrote on his Truth Social account.
"Dana, please take the job!" Trump said, calling on the longtime fight promoter to bring "assistants" with him "even though some are not from our country."
Dana White has been president of the UFC since 2001 and its CEO since 2023.
The White House does not have a press secretary as yet.
Katie Zacharia left the high-profile job on October 16 after a shaky debut press briefing. She was out as press secretary in less than a week after her appointment to the job.

articles.title: Paraguay prosecutors charge impeached ex-president Peña, seek pre-trail detention
articles.summary: Paraguayan prosecutors on Saturday charged former president Santiago Peña with breach of trust and administration for personal gain and asked a court to jail him pending trial, a day after his…

image.caption: Paraguay's former president Santiago Peña, left, arrives at the Attorney General’s Office to appear before prosecutors in in Asunción, Paraguay, on Saturday. (Fiscalia Paraguay/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Paraguayan prosecutors on Saturday charged former president Santiago Peña with breach of trust and administration for personal gain and asked a court to jail him pending trial, a day after his ​impeachment over the collapse of digital lender Ueno.
Santiago Peña charged with breach of trust, administration for personal gain

Prosecutors also ​charged former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo with breach of trust, producing false public documents and administration for personal gain, and sought his pretrial detention. Prosecutors ​said Peña should serve pretrial detention at a location determined by the ⁠court, if the judge ⁠orders it.
Peña's attorney did not immediately respond ‌to a request for comment, nor did Carvallo.

Prosecutors allege that Peña used his position as president to influence decisions by government agencies and state-owned entities to keep large amounts of public money deposited at Ueno, despite maintaining financial ties to the ⁠lender. They say that relationship created a conflict of interest as Peña encouraged, facilitated or influenced decisions benefiting the bank.
Peña, who was a shareholder in Ueno’s holding company until March 2025, has denied wrongdoing ‌and said the bank's problems were a regulatory matter.

Peña had arrived at the Attorney General’s Office earlier on Saturday to appear before prosecutors following his dramatic removal from power on Friday. His ouster brought Vice President Pedro Alliana to power, with the ​longtime ruling Colorado Party politician sworn in on Friday to complete Peña’s term through August 2028.
The two charges against Peña ⁠could carry a sentence of up to 10 years in prison each, the prosecutor said.
Carvallo ⁠resigned as central bank chief earlier this week as the crisis surrounding Ueno escalated. He ⁠had ⁠previously headed the digital lender until ​2023.

The collapse has left millions of customers struggling to access their accounts and prompted protests in Asunción. The scandal has also swept ⁠up senior officials and former Ueno executives, while regulators have sought to reassure markets and contain risks to the wider financial system.
The central bank on Saturday said the equivalent of $160 million US had been paid out to nearly 1.2 million savers, under the state deposit guarantee scheme.

articles.title: France sees new round of Yellow Vest, student protests
articles.summary: Although fewer protesters turned out in comparison with previous weeks, several cities saw clashes between police and demonstrators.

image.caption: Police deployed tear gas in the evening to disperse protesters in ParisImage: Stephanie Lecocq/REUTERS

blocks.text: Fewer protesters than expected turned out for the fourth weekend of mass demonstrations in France, although clashes with police were reported in several cities, the Interior Ministry said on Saturday.
Authorities had expected up to 170,000 people to protest nationwide, including 60,000 in Paris.

The ministry reported a slightly lower nationwide total of 146,000 people, out of which some 46,000 took to the streets of the French capital, where the afternoon was reported to have remained mostly calm, with some isolated incidents reported in the evening involving the deployment of tear gas.
Protest organizers gave a higher nationwide count of over 250,000 protesters, which is nevertheless fewer than the 320,000 to 500,000 that were reported to have turned out last Saturday.
Clashes between police and protesters were reported in Toulouse, Marseille, Lyon and Bordeaux.
The Interior Ministry reported some 350 arrests nationwide by the evening in connection with the protests.

blocks.caption: Trash cans were set on fire in MarseilleImage: Justine Meddah/AFP

blocks.text: Fourth week of protests in France
Students and labor unions had called an authorized central Paris march "against the high cost of living and in support of young people."

blocks.caption: A protest march began at Place de la Republique SatursdayImage: Stephanie Lecocq/REUTERS

blocks.text: In Paris, an authorized march proceeded peacefully from Republique to Nation, but tensions erupted after police said some 200 "violent individuals" attacked law enforcement after a man was arrested for setting fire to a trash can, according to Paris' police headquarters.

blocks.caption: Depsite several incidents, French authorities said the protests in Paris were mostly calmImage: Stephanie Lecocq/REUTERS

blocks.text: Separately, the country's so-called "Yellow Vest" movement — which gained notoriety eight years ago by violently protesting a proposed fuel tax hike rejected invitations to join the student rally.

Instead, the "Gilets Jaunes" held a banned event at Paris' Place de la Concorde, close to parliament and the presidential Elysee Palace. Two of its leading figures, Benjamin Ball and Solene Azelma Sigaux, were arrested and taken into custody.

Ahead of Saturday's protests, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said 70,000 police and security forces would be deployed across the country over the weekend, adding that authorities will "be ready" for "rioters and looters."
France protests turn violent nationwide
Can France afford to raise wages, invest in schools?

The large police presence comes on the heels of weeks of mass demonstrations that have at times grown extremely violent, most notably on October 17, when France's worst rioting in years resulted in more than a billion euros in damage to private and public property.
On Thursday, police made over 600 arrests during a nationwide strike that included blockades and other protest action.
Authorities say that, for the most part, protests have remained peaceful.

But there have continued to be numerous incidents of violent clashes with police, as outgoing President Emmanuel Macron and his government struggle to address public discontent over the rising cost of living.

Although Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is scheduled to meet with trade and employee unions on Monday, organizers say the only thing that will quell anger will be for the government to bow to their demands.

"The only thing that will bring the protests to an end is a response to the demands that have been put forward for several weeks by workers, civil servants, young people and pensioners," according to an inter-union coalition statement published on Friday.
This latest round of protests began with students calling for improvements to the national education system and unions joining in to call for wage hikes and tax reforms.

Macron's government has said it intends to raise the minimum wage as well as increase funding for schools and teaching staff. But it finds itself in a tight fiscal spot as debt — currently 119% of GDP — continues to run out of control in the EU's second-largest economy.
Could France's debt crisis spread across Europe?

articles.title: How do you broker UN climate talks when your own country is a big coal and gas exporter? Chris Bowen is about to find out
articles.summary:
Ahead of Cop31, climate change minister dismisses concerns about whether Australia as a major producer can keep the world moving away from fossil fuels

  • Listen to the podcast:
articles.byline: Graham Readfearn Environment and climate correspondent

blocks.text: Australia has been urged to set aside support for its near US$100bn fossil fuel export industries and fight for a global agreement to move away from coal, gas and oil as its climate change minister, Chris Bowen, leads negotiations between nearly 200 countries at UN talks this week.

Delegates will gather in the Turkish Mediterranean resort city of Antalya on Monday for Cop31, two weeks of climate talks held amid geopolitical turmoil, with conflict in the Middle East driving an oil price crisis that has raised living costs across the globe.

The talks – which open two months after climate scientists confirmed global heating would reach at least 1.8C – will seek support for a new 2035 electrification goal, backed by Turkey and Australia, to have 35% of final energy use around the world coming from electricity instead of fossil fuels.

Australia is the world’s second largest exporter of coal for burning in power stations and the largest exporter of coal for steelmaking. About one fifth of the world’s liquefied natural gas exports also come from its shores – on par with Qatar, but behind the world’s biggest exporter, the United States. The government expects the export value of the three fuels to be $141bn (US$98bn) this financial year.
Turkey and Australia vied for hosting rights and came to a compromise with Turkey as president of the conference and Australia president of the negotiations themselves.

Bowen, the Cop31 president of negotiations, will try to somehow find consensus across rich fossil fuel producers such as Saudi Arabia and Russia and emerging economic giants – including the world’s biggest emitter, China – and poorer vulnerable countries for whom climate change is seen as an existential threat.

Speaking to the Guardian on Thursday, Bowen highlighted three areas of focus: minimising overshoot past the 1.5C Paris agreement temperature goal; helping poorer countries to access enough finance to deal with the climate crisis; and the new electrification goal. Ocean protection is likely to be another major theme.
Climate advocates have questioned if, as a major fossil fuel producer, Australia can keep the world moving away from fossil fuels.
Bowen dismissed that notion, saying all countries were dealing with the transition and Australia’s domestic moves away from coal in electricity had been recognised internationally.
Not on the official Cop31 agenda is any mention of countries developing detailed plans to transition away from fossil fuels – a step seen by climate experts as central to limiting the crisis.

blocks.caption: Turkey’s Murat Kurum and Bowen with Fiji’s Lynda Tabuya (left) and the UN’s Simon Stiell (right) at the Pacific Pre-Cop31 summit in Fiji. Photograph: Saeed Khan/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The Australian scientist Bill Hare, the chief executive of Climate Analytics and veteran Cop attender, said countries agreed at the 2023 summit that a transition was needed and the president of last year’s climate summit, Brazil, had progressed calls for countries to develop plans to leave fossil fuels behind, even when it couldn’t find consensus at the talks.
“Australia could pitch this up – to continue this process of developing a fossil fuel roadmap. Australia could do that,” said Hare.
“Why should this process stop? That’s a hard political question for Australia to answer. I think [Bowen] needs to be brave at this Cop.”
Brazil published the first global fossil fuel roadmap this week but experts pointed to a lack of benchmarks or timelines.
Hare said a “critical issue” at Cop31 was to address the 1.5C overshoot.

“Fossil fuels are critical to that because they are about 75% of global emissions. We can’t limit overshoot without a very rapid transition away from fossil fuels. Whatever the theatre of the talks is, this has to be the central point.”

Climate and energy policy is divisive in Australia with the conservative Coalition, in opposition, pledging to scrap the 2050 net zero emissions target, and the rightwing populist party One Nation rejecting the science of climate change entirely. Both are vocal in their objections to renewable energy projects.
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, will need to thread this political needle when he speaks during a two-day leaders summit at the talks.
after newsletter promotion
Cover decision

Turkey and Australia want the talks to end with an overarching agreement from all countries – known as a cover decision. The UN talks work by consensus, meaning every country must agree before resolutions are passed.

Prof Frank Jotzo, an economist and climate policy expert at the Australian National University, said he doubted all participants would agree on mapping a route away from fossil fuels because “those countries that want to keep that out of the process will simply prevail in having that struck off the agenda”.
“The Australian government will want to play this very safe,” he said. “I think the Australian presidency will have a strong focus on an orderly procedure with no surprises.”

blocks.caption: Preparations for this week’s Cop31 conference in Antalya. Photograph: Sandro Basili/Shutterstock

blocks.text: More than 500 mostly Australian scientists and academics wrote to Albanese this week pleading for an end to coal and gas approvals and asking for a legislated plan to phase out fossil fuel production that protects workers and communities.

“Australia cannot credibly lead on climate abroad nor ensure national nor regional security while it expands coal and gas at home,” the letter said. “We ask you to be brave, to be bold, and to act with the urgency that the evidence demands.”
They wrote that championing access to climate finance while approving new coal and gas projects “invites the charge of hypocrisy”.

Kathryn McCallum, the director of strategy at the Climate Action Network Australia, said the Albanese government had approved 38 coal, oil and gas projects since it was elected in 2022. Those developments include extending the life of one of the biggest gas projects on the planet – Woodside’s giant North West Shelf processing facility in Western Australia – until 2070.

“Australia has the opportunity to play a climate leadership role, but as one of the biggest producers and exporters that’s expanding coal and gas production at an enormous scale, it doesn’t pass the pub test to talk about limiting overshoot while approving corporate proposals for new coal and gas,” McCallum said.
“A lot of people are asking if Australia is serious [about climate action] because of these approvals.
“Australia will be right in the spotlight. The Australian government needs to stand up to the corporations that want to export this coal and gas, and act in the global interest.”

articles.title: A Big Build royal commission helped Ben Carroll become premier. Will it be his downfall?
articles.summary:
Two weeks of public hearings will begin on Monday morning, right in the middle of the state election campaign

  • Get our

blocks.text: The commitment that made Ben Carroll premier may ultimately cost him the election.
On Monday morning, right in the middle of a state election campaign, the royal commission into Victoria’s Big Build will begin two weeks of public hearings.

For Labor, this is the worst possible timing. It wants to be talking about anything other than allegations of corruption and criminal infiltration of government projects. For the Coalition, it is a gift they will exploit.
Carroll – whose campaign bus is splashed with the words “new premier, new direction” – will face sustained questions about the actions of his predecessors and a past he wants to move away from.
Labor insiders fear the next two weeks could be damaging.
“If there are bad news stories, Ben will be up in the media and we will not change our plan,” says a senior Labor source.
“He’ll say ‘I set this up, I want answers’. Ben is owning it. The campaign will own it.”
In reality, they have little choice.

Calling this inquiry – formally known as the Royal Commission into the Integrity of Major Public and Civil Infrastructure Construction Projects – may have been Carroll’s first decision as premier. But he has no control over when hearings are held and who is called.
His premiership is also intrinsically tied to this royal commission.
When his predecessor, Jacinta Allan, refused to call it, despite admitting criminals had infiltrated construction projects, her party room turned to someone who would.
When Carroll walked into Government House as writs for the election were issued, he said: “I want to be a premier that did what he said he would do on integrity.”

So far, this has earned him respect from one of Victorian Labor’s most persistent critics. Deborah Glass served as the state’s ombudsman from 2014 to 2024, and publicly called for a royal commission in June, weeks before Allan resigned.
“This is a necessary examination of a shameful chapter in Victoria’s history,” Glass tells Guardian Australia.
“Ben Carroll has shown political courage setting up a royal commission whose proceedings will no doubt be painful not only for his predecessors but his party.”
That pain was made clear earlier this week, when some of the early submissions to the royal commission were aired in the media.

William McDougall, a planning expert with five decades of experience on Victorian government projects, said in his submission that Labor advisers may have influenced major projects without transparency or accountability.
McDougall’s submission delivered a scathing assessment of how Labor has managed the Big Build. He argues “announcement precedes analysis, dissent is discouraged, and accountability is weakened”.

“Such a system increases the risk of selecting inferior projects, misallocating public funds, suppressing professional advice and creating conditions in which misconduct can flourish,” McDougall’s submission says.
after newsletter promotion

These claims are denied by the government, and will ultimately be tested by the royal commission. But they are politically damaging. So too are headlines linking Labor to a key player in the Big Build scandal: the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU).
On Friday, the commission revealed its initial focus would include the CFMEU’s conduct on rail projects in Sunbury.

In 2024 the then Victorian CFMEU boss, John Setka, quit after 12 years at the helm after a Nine investigation unearthed a raft of misconduct allegations that detailed how some of the highest-ranking bikie bosses had been parachuted into union delegate positions on the Big Build.
In August, Roy Morgan polling of 2,084 Victorians found “corruption and integrity failures” were the top issues that would stop people voting for Labor.

blocks.caption: Carroll steps off his campaign bus. If Labor loses the election, as polls predict, the royal commission will be his lasting legacy. Photograph: Rob Prezioso/AAP

blocks.text: This may be one reason why there are still some Labor MPs who would prefer this was not happening. They argue Allan failed to appropriately respond to the allegations when they were first aired by the Nine newspapers in 2024. If she had, political damage could have been limited.

Carroll knew these MPs and sections of the union movement would not be happy. While the MPs have toed the line, some unions have broken away. Labor concedes the Electrical Trades Union’s decision not to fund Labor’s campaign could be costly.
If Labor loses this election, as polls predict, the royal commission will be Carroll’s lasting legacy.
But the Liberals could use the commission to inflict more pain on Labor and the broader union movement.
The party has plans to expand its remit to explicitly investigate all trade unions, as well as political and financial incentives behind the Big Build.
Whatever chaos unfolds in coming weeks, and whoever wins on 28 November, Glass remains hopeful the commission will deliver a forensic analysis of what went wrong and why.
“While a proper examination will inevitably take time, Victorians need answers to those questions as soon as possible.”

articles.title: Armenia's selective prosecution: A threat to EU relations?
articles.summary: While Brussels has refrained from harsh criticism, Armenian civil society has warned of selective justice against opposition figures. Could the EU's pragmatic stance risk repeating past mistakes?

image.caption: Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan's government has positioned Armenia as an increasingly close partner of the European Union in the South CaucasusImage: Anthony Pizzoferrato/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: In early October, Artur Danielyan, leader of Armenia's opposition party Adekvad, was arrested following a Facebook post criticizing Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan.
The incident is part of a growing trend: Over the past two years, Armenian authorities have brought charges against multiple opposition figures, largely based on their social media activity.
Civil society representatives warn that such selective justice signals a worrying turn toward democratic backsliding.
The arrest of Artur Danielyan
The grounds for Danielyan's detention were Facebook posts in which he criticized both Pashinyan and the country's security services.

One point of contention was Pashinyan's stance on a possible prisoner exchange involving an Azerbaijani soldier accused of breaking into the home of a 39-year-old woman in the Armenian village of Shaki and injuring her and her children.

In an interview with Armenian news outlet Infocom, Pashinyan ruled out swapping the soldier imprisoned in Armenia for detained Armenians in Azerbaijan. Danielyan responded with a scathing attack, calling the prime minister a "scumbag" and accusing him of being unwilling to bring his fellow citizens home.

Armenia and Azerbaijan were in conflict for three decades over Nagorno-Karabakh, a breakaway Azerbaijani region populated by Armenians that declared independence in the 1990s. After Azerbaijan's military offensive in 2023, Baku regained control over the territory, forcing over 100,000 Armenians to flee. Currently, 19 Armenian individuals are being detained in Baku, including former high-ranking officials from Nagorno-Karabakh's de facto administration.

blocks.caption: Artur Danielyan, leader of the far-right "Adekvat" party, is a controversial figure in ArmeniaImage: Alexander Ryumin/TASS/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Growing trend of selective prosecutions?
Over a dozen Armenian civil society organizations have condemned the prosecution of the Adekvad party leader, calling it "patently illegal, disproportionate, and politically motivated."
"It is punitive in nature and sends a direct signal to the broader public aimed at silencing dissent, critical views, and undesirable speech", said the joint statement.
Several other criminal proceedings have been launched against activists who criticized the ruling establishment or Pashinyan.

Another prominent case emerged ahead of the parliamentary elections in June. Artur Osipyan, a displaced activist from Nagorno-Karabakh, was arrested after a verbal clash with Pashinyan over his Nagorno-Karabakh policy.

Following the incident, Armenian prosecutors indicted Osipyan for disrupting public order and obstructing the ruling party's campaign. He was also charged with inciting violence against Pashinyan in a social media post from March.
Is freedom of expression in danger in Armenia?
On April 15, 2020, Article 226.2 was added to the Criminal Code of Armenia, penalizing public calls to violence, as well as the public justification or promotion of violence.

After strong outrage by civil society, these offences were subsequently decriminalized. According to a 2025 report by Freedom House, "nearly 95% of court cases concerning incitement to violence under a 2020 criminal code amendment had involved alleged threats against Prime Minister Pashinyan and his supporters, whereas potentially prohibited statements by ruling party members were apparently not subject to the same scrutiny."

Throughout the 2026 pre-election period, the Regional Center for Democracy and Security (RCDS), an independent think tank based in Yerevan, monitored online hate speech targeting Nagorno-Karabakh refugees.

Their reports documented how pro-government bloggers and influential social media users used their platforms to direct hostile rhetoric toward displaced Karabakh Armenians, labeling them with derogatory terms. Despite these findings, law enforcement agencies in Armenia largely refrained from pursuing criminal prosecutions against these activists.
Why doesn't the EU react?
Despite Armenia's efforts to strengthen its ties with the EU, Brussels has given no clear response to the silencing of opposition voices, observers in Yerevan told DW.
"The EU, by and large, has adopted a very pragmatic and geopolitically driven approach," said political analyst Tigran Grigoryan.

"Given various regional developments, including what is happening in Georgia, Armenia has now become the EU's primary partner in the region," he added. "Coupled with the fact that the alternative to Pashinyan is a pro-Russian opposition, there is ultimately no serious response to these criminal cases."

Stefan Meister, Eastern Europe expert at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP), echoed this view. European support for Armenia appears to be "mainly driven by the European Russia policy," Meister said. "So it's not so much about Armenia itself, but it is more about strengthening those forces that are undermining Russia's influence in the country and in the region."

He believes that Pashinyan leverages this geopolitical dynamic to label internal political opponents as Russian proxies. However, not everyone who criticizes Pashinyan is pro-Russian, Meister added. He pointed out that "the EU is somehow falling into this trap by accepting that this is the right narrative."
EU: Armenia should deliver on its commitment

Democracy, the rule of law, and fundamental rights are at the core of the EU-Armenia Comprehensive and Enhanced Partnership Agreement (CEPA) and the Strategic Agenda for the EU-Armenia Partnership, an EU spokesperson said in a written response to DW's request for comment.

It also pointed out that "the EU is closely following developments in the country, including as regards criminal investigations. In line with Armenia's international commitments and legal framework, such investigations should be carried out in an independent and impartial manner, free from political considerations."

articles.title: What we know about Krakow mass shooting so far
articles.summary: At least six people were killed by a gunman in military fatigues who opened fire in Poland's second largest city.

blocks.text: Image source, Agencja Wyborcza.pl/Reuters
ByFlorence Freeman and Emer Moreau

At least six people have been killed and several others injured after a gunman opened fire in central Krakow, the second largest city in Poland. Details are still emerging - here is everything we know so far.
How did the attack unfold?
The attack began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in Krakow's Main Market Square, the bustling central point of the city.
Police said a man drove into the square before beginning to fire "at random people from his car".
Footage from the scene shows scenes of panic as people fled, with the sound of gunfire clearly heard.

items: Follow live updates from Krakow

blocks.text: People run for shelter as gunshots heard in Krakow
Armed officers raced to the scene and engaged in a gunfight with the attacker.
The gunman was shot but is alive and has been arrested.
Distressing footage authenticated by BBC Verify shows the moment a police officer confronts the suspect on the ground before firing his weapon several times.
The officer then falls to the ground, apparently having been injured himself.
Moment police officer appears to shoot Krakow suspect
Shop windows in the square have signs of damage, seemingly from bullets, with glass shards scattered along the floor.
City officials have urged people who live in the city and tourists to stay away from the area while an investigation continues.
How many people have died and been injured?
Six people - four women and two men - are confirmed to have been killed.
At least 15 people have been injured, including two police officers who were shot while detaining the attacker.

One of the police officers was described as being in a "very critical condition" by a Polish government minister after being shot three times while arresting the attacker. The officer is undergoing surgery, he added.
Polish authorities have not confirmed the names and ages of the other victims.

blocks.caption: A map showing Krakow Main Square Market

blocks.text: What do we know about the suspect and motive?
Police have confirmed the attacker was a male Polish citizen but no further details about his identity have been released.
The suspect was wearing "military-style attire" and had a military-grade weapon, according to a police spokesperson
"Many pieces of weapons and ammunition were found in his vehicle", the spokesperson added.
Nothing has been publicly confirmed about the motive behind the attack so far.
How did witnesses describe the attack?
The shooting happened in one of the largest medieval squares in Europe, a busy location which is also a popular tourist destination.
Jonathan Balshaw from Ipswich was there with his Polish girlfriend Dominika. The couple were outside St Mary's Basilica, in the corner of the square, when the shooting started.
Jonathan said: "We ran down the side of the church and through the side door and hid with several other people until the gunfire died down.
"A lot of shots were fired, more than 20 with it sounding like multiple different firearms - there were two distinctly different noises."
Caitlin Shasby from Newcastle arrived in Krakow yesterday with her friend Jon for a long weekend.
She said they heard shots from their hotel room but were not sure what was happening until their hotel rang them and told them to "stay in our rooms until further notice".
Moment shooting heard in Krakow square
What has the reaction been in Poland and internationally?
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk is on his way to Krakow and is expected to give an address later on Saturday.
Earlier, he said he was being kept informed by the interior minister and that police were investigating "the background and all the circumstances".
President Karol Nawrocki said he was "deeply concerned" and was awaiting "a full explanation of the circumstances surrounding these tragic events".
US ambassador to Poland Tom Rose described it as a "savage and murderous attack".
The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the shooting was "a tragedy that will be felt far beyond Poland".

articles.title: US offers $20m reward for information about Iran's nuclear programme
articles.summary: Donald Trump has repeatedly raised the prospecting of renewing strikes against Iran's nuclear facilities.

blocks.text: A US State Department statement about its multi-million dollar reward said it was offering the money for information about the Iranian programme, including "facilities, equipment and associated personnel".

It said Iran's "lack of compliance with the IAEA [the International Atomic Energy Agency] on safeguards obligations has led to the agency's loss of 'continuity of knowledge' regarding Iran's production and inventory of key components like [nuclear] centrifuges".
Centrifuges are needed to produce enriched uranium, which can be used to make reactor fuel for civilian use but also for nuclear weapons if enriched to around 90% purity or higher.

There had been mounting speculation that the US might resume significant strikes in Iran after the midterm elections, though Trump told reporters, prior to the polls, that he was in "no rush" to do so.
In an interview with Fox News on the eve of the midterms, the president also said the US "might need to go after Pickaxe [Mountain]", an underground site linked to Iran's nuclear programme.
This was "not a big deal" and could be done in "one hour", Trump said.
The president has repeatedly threatened to bomb the suspected underground site on previous occasions.

However, both Trump and Vice-President JD Vance have said public opposition to the war on Iran fuelled heavy losses for their Republican Party in this week's midterm elections, which has led to speculation the White House may no longer seek an escalation in the conflict.
On Friday, Trump insisted that Iran was keen to end the eight-month conflict with the US, stressing the damage to Tehran's economy and military.
"We're dealing with them now. They want to make a deal very badly," he said.
Qatar's foreign ministry spokesman said on Tuesday that both sides were "reviewing the ideas and proposals we have presented" and that it remained hopeful of a deal being agreed.
Iranian negotiators had discussed with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days once the US met its seven conditions.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

articles.title: South Africa's ANC facing worst-ever performance in local elections
articles.summary: Near-final results show South Africa's once dominant ANC will see its lowest-ever vote percentage. The party is taking the blame for shoddy municipal services, including water and electricity…

image.caption: Millions of South Africans headed to the polls across the country's municipalities to elect local councilors and mayors (Photo: November 4)Image: Leandre Steenberg/Matrix Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: South Africa's African National Congress (ANC) is heading for an historically poor election performance, with the near-final tally from Wednesday's municipal polls showing it coming in with just over 30% of the vote.
The ANC also lost its majority in six of the eight metropolitan regions, South Africa's Electoral Commission said Saturday in sharing the results after 98% of votes were counted.

South African voters in 2026 are angry about water and electricity shortages, with the ANC taking the blame for the poor state of municipalities. High unemployment, crime, and widespread corruption are other pressing issues.

ANC leader, and South African president, Cyril Ramaphosa, has not yet addressed the poor performance as of Saturday evening. However, during the week, he admitted in his weekly presidential letter that "municipal failures have contributed to declining public trust and confidence in democratic governance."
On Saturday, ANC Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula told reporters that the ANC needs to work on winning back public confidence.
"We cannot ask the people to trust us merely because of our history," Mbalula said.
"This has been a very catastrophic outcome for the ANC ... as much as we are the largest party, it has been catastrophic for the movement," he added.
The ANC's steady decline with voters

Although the ANC will still be the single largest party by overall vote percentage, it had governed with an absolute majority for most of its history up until the general election in 2024 saw it lose an outright parliamentary majority for the first time in South Africa's democratic era.
"This is the most severe result that the ANC would have feared," political analyst Daniel Silke told the AFP news agency.

"It's the ANC's worst result in history," Silke said, adding that the result will undermine the ANC's ability to exert authority on the local and national level. The results could also provide a bellwether of voter sentiment ahead of the 2029 general elections.
Once led by Nelson Mandela, the ANC was instrumental in ending apartheid, and took and power in 1994 after South Africa became a democracy.

But over the past decade, it has steadily performed worse in one election after another. In 2024, the ANC secured just over 40% in the 2024 national polls and 46% at the previous municipal elections in 2021.
After losing the absolute majority in 2024, the ANC formed a cross-party national unity government with all the parties represented in parliament, which is still in power.

The ANC's decline comes amid disillusionment over corruption, mismanagement and high unemployment. Smaller parties have also emerged across South Africa's political landscape, cutting into the ANC's voter base.
DA opposition holds large cities
South Africa is now looking at complex coalition negotiations for municipal level governing alliances.
Runner up in the polls looks to be the pro-business, center-right Democratic Alliance (DA), coming in at 24% of the votes.

The DA is set to keep control of Cape Town after winning an absolute majority. It also performed well in the capital, Pretoria, and economic hub of Johannesburg, and is expected to form coalitions that exclude the ANC.

"All of the cut and thrust that comes with the election is now over, and it is time now... to put together governments that can actually fix these towns and cities," DA leader Geordin Hill-Lewis told reporters.
"We have already reached out to many parties over the last 24 hours and will continue to do so today," he said.

articles.title: LTO summons bus driver, operator after engine cover kills pedestrian in Quezon
articles.summary: The Land Transportation Office (LTO) has issued a show-cause order (SCO) against the driver and operator of a passenger bus involved in the death of a pedestrian in Atimonan, Quezon.

blocks.text: Published November 8, 2026 2:05am
The Land Transportation Office (LTO) has issued a show-cause order (SCO) against the driver and operator of a passenger bus involved in the death of a pedestrian in Atimonan, Quezon.
The incident occurred at around 5 a.m. on November 5, 2026, along the northbound lane of Maharlika Highway in Barangay Tagbakin, the LTO said in a news release.

According to a police report, the bus was traversing the highway when its engine cover suddenly detached while the vehicle was moving and hit a pedestrian standing by the roadside while waiting for a ride to Manila.
The victim sustained serious injuries and was rushed to Doña Marta Hospital. The victim was declared dead on arrival.
The LTO identified the bus driver and operator and formally served them with the SCO, according to LTO chief Assistant Secretary Markus Lacanilao

Under the order, the driver and operator are required to appear before the LTO Central Office's Intelligence and Investigation Division (IID) on November 13 to submit their sworn statements and explanations, along with supporting documents, regarding the alleged violation of reckless driving.
The bus operator is also facing charges of employing a reckless driver and breach of franchise conditions.
The LTO said the driver's license may be suspended or revoked if the agency's final decision finds him to be an improper person to operate a motor vehicle.
As part of its immediate action, the agency ordered the driver to surrender his license to the IID for a 90-day suspension. The bus has also been placed under alarm.

"Negligence in maintaining a passenger bus in good condition should never result in the loss of life. Every part and component of a vehicle must be ensured to be safe and in proper working condition before it travels, as even a single oversight can lead to a road tragedy," Lacanilao said.
The LTO assured the public that those found violating transportation laws and regulations would be held accountable.
It also vowed to intensify its monitoring of the roadworthiness of public utility vehicles to prevent similar incidents and protect the lives of all road users. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Six dead after gunman opens fire ‘at random’ in Kraków market square
articles.summary: Reports say man fired shots from from his car in Poland’s second city before being wounded by police while trying to flee

blocks.text: Six people have been killed and 15 injured after a shooting in a market square in Kraków, Poland.
A man who had driven into the square at about 3pm began “firing at random people from his car”, according to a statement by local police on X.
The gunman was a Polish citizen who acted alone and was shot and wounded during a gunfight with police nearby, authorities said.
He used a long military-type firearm, the police said.
Police officers are among the wounded.

blocks.caption: Five killed in Krakow market square shooting

blocks.text: The incident took place in the main market square, a popular tourist destination in Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city.

A tram driver reported about 3pm that his vehicle was shot at from a man in a moving car while passing nearby the main square, the Krakow municipal transport company said. The window to the tram driver’s cabin was shattered.
The prime minister, Donald Tusk, confirmed the shooting after initial reports by local media, which cited police and the fire department.

“I am being kept informed by the minister of the interior about the situation in Kraków following the tragic shooting,” he wrote on X, adding that “the police are investigating the background and all the circumstances of the attack”.
Later in the evening, government spokesperson Adam Szlapka wrote on X: “Today’s event in Kraków has shaken all of Poland,” adding that “Prime minister Donald Tusk is on his way to Kraków”
after newsletter promotion
The justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, wrote on X that authorities would “ensure that the perpetrator of this crime is held fully accountable and severely punished”.
The Polish president, Karol Nawrocki, said he was “deeply concerned by reports of the tragic events” in Kraków, and that his thoughts are with victims, those injured and their families.
An interior minister is heading to the scene, according to reports.
Earlier this year, Euronews reported that the number of legally owned firearms in Poland surpassed 1 million for the first time.

Poland issued a record 50,700 gun permits in 2025, and the number of active permits registered in 2025 was almost double the number registered in 2015, according to the police statistics cited in the report.

articles.title: Houthis say at least 25 killed in Saudi air strike
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia, which leads a coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen, has not commented.

blocks.text: Media linked to the Houthi movement in Yemen say that at least 25 people, including women and children, have been killed in airstrikes by Saudi Arabia.
There has been no comment from the Saudi-led coalition backing the internationally recognised government in Yemen.

Live video footage on Al Masirah - a television station run by the Houthis - has shown rescuers pulling bodies out of the rubble of several buildings in al-Shariyah, a town to the east of the capital, Sanaa.
The bodies of young children can be seen among those dug out from the ruins.
The television station has also shown a number of injured people being carried on stretchers to hospital.
Saba news agency, which is also run by the Houthis, said the attack was carried out by Saudi Arabia.
The Saudis have led a coalition that has been fighting the Houthis for more than a decade in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government.
The war in Yemen had been dormant for several years but reignited as a result of the Iran war.
A truce began to fall apart when Saudi Arabia struck the airport in Sanaa - which is controlled by the Houthis - to prevent an Iranian plan landing there.

The Tehran-backed Houthis subsequently targeted Abha airport in Saudi Arabia, then began hitting Saudi ships that have been using the Red Sea off the coast of Yemen as an alternative oil export route to the Strait of Hormuz.
Major fighting has since resumed in Yemen between the Houthis and forces fighting for the Saudi-backed government of Yemen.
On Friday, an attack on a market in Taiz province, which has been the focus of much of the recent fighting, is reported to have killed 30 people.
The Houthis accused the Saudis of carrying out the strike, while government forces accused the Houthis of having fired a missile at the site.
The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed.
The Saudis have regularly bombed Houthi positions, while the group has fired multiple missiles at targets inside Saudi Arabia, including airports and oil facilities.
Hours before the strike that hit al-Shariyah, the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a missile heading towards Riyadh.
A Houthi leader, Mahdi al-Mashat, has vowed that the group will take revenge for the latest attacks in Yemen.

articles.title: Rise in NHS birth centre closures ‘shocking’ denial of women’s rights, experts say
articles.summary:
Twelve midwife-led maternity units have closed in England since 2019 with six closing since Labour came to power in 2024

NHS officials are shutting growing numbers of birth centres in a…

blocks.text: NHS officials are shutting growing numbers of birth centres in a “shocking” denial of a woman’s right to have a midwife rather than a doctor oversee their baby’s birth, say campaigners.

Twelve birth centres – midwife-led maternity units – have closed in England since 2019. Birth centres play a key role in ensuring that women can choose whether to have their baby at a unit in a hospital run by doctors, at one where midwives are in charge, or at home.

Six units have shut permanently since Labour came to power in July 2024. Four others have been closed “temporarily” for so long, up to six years, that childbirth groups fear they will never reopen. Two other birth centres closed because the hospitals where they were based have begun to fall apart and will remain out of action for several years until new facilities are built.
Women’s ability to choose where their baby is born is also being increasingly restricted in England and Wales by NHS bodies suspending home birth services for up to 14 months.
The wave of closures and suspensions is occurring because of the NHS-wide shortage of midwives, a falling birthrate, the growing complexity of childbirth and a rise in caesarean sections.
Campaigners say the loss of local childbirth services is denying women their right to choose and forcing them to travel from their home area to give birth.

The Royal College of Midwives said that women’s inability to access midwife-led care on the NHS risks them deciding to pay for private midwifery support or even have a baby at home with no health professional present.

Hazel Williams, the chief executive of Birthrights, said: “Over the past few years we have seen shocking restrictions on women and birthing people’s choices of place of birth, with more and more birth centre closures and restrictions and the option for NHS-supported home birth vastly reduced for many.
“These are not luxury options or nice-to-haves. This is about women and birthing people’s right to choose what happens to their bodies and their birth.”

The six permanent closures during Labour’s time in government have been in Rossendale, east Lancashire; Edgware in north London; Melton Mowbray in Leicestershire; Stafford and Lichfield in Staffordshire; and Pontefract in West Yorkshire. NHS bodies that have decided to close birth centres often stress they do not have enough midwives to staff the service safely.

Tope Medupin, the acting chief executive of the National Childbirth Trust, said: “For women and birthing people the loss of a local service often means longer journeys, higher costs, greater uncertainty and fewer options for care at one of the most important times in their lives.

“Longstanding workforce shortages, crumbling estates and wider pressures on maternity services remain unresolved and women are increasingly expected to travel further for maternity care as a result. That cannot simply become the new normal.”

The Huddersfield birth centre in Yorkshire closed in November 2020 as a temporary measure because of the Covid-19 pandemic. But six years later it has not reopened. “No decision has been made to reopen the service and we are not able to provide a timeframe for any potential reopening,” said the Calderdale and Huddersfield NHS trust which ran it. “Any future decisions will be based on a thorough assessment of clinical safety, workforce sustainability and the needs of local women and families.”
Similarly, Ingleside birth centre in Salford, which opened in 2018, has been shut – again ostensibly as a temporary step – since January 2022.

Midwife-led births at the birth centre in Crowborough, east Sussex, were halted temporarily in October 2025 because staff shortages meant it kept closing at short notice. Maidstone and Tunbridge Wells NHS trust, which runs the centre, said it had completed a review of what it would take to reopen the facility but declined to say what that would involve.
The MP for Sussex Weald, Nusrat Ghani, who is campaigning for it to reopen, said the NHS trust had broken “numerous promises” to review the practicalities of reopening the service.

“We have had thousands of local mums and residents complain at the closure of the service and the trust is ignoring their health needs and choices,” Ghani said. “I am disappointed that the trust doesn’t give weight to the prospect of avoidable complications for mothers who are having to travel for up to 90 minutes to give birth.”
The trust may be continuing to describe the closure as temporary to avoid the formal public consultation it would have to undertake if it were made permanent, Ghani suggested.
Gloucester hospitals trust announced last week that Cheltenham birth centre will reopen in February after being shut since 2022 and that home births, suspended since 2025, will resume in January.
A senior NHS leader recently warned that up to 20 full-scale, consultant-led maternity units at acute hospitals in England may have to close in order to keep women and babies safe.

There are fears that the birth centres at the Queen Elizabeth hospital in King’s Lynn and James Paget hospital in Great Yarmouth could also shut after NHS bosses in Norfolk last week proposed closing their maternity units and instead centralising care for the county at the Norfolk and Norwich University hospital in Norwich.
The maternity unit at North Devon district hospital in Barnstaple has been closed for months, including its home birth service, due to lack of staff.

Hannah Leonard, the chief policy officer and deputy chief midwife at the Royal College of Midwives, said: “Women have the right to choose where they give birth, but that choice is being eroded. The evidence shows that for some women choosing to give birth in a birth centre or at home improves outcomes and experience for the woman and her baby.”
Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, is due to publish an action plan to address the crisis in maternity and neonatal care in England before Christmas.

The Department of Health and Social Care did not respond directly to the closures. A spokesperson said: “Every woman and baby deserves safe, compassionate maternity and neonatal care and the health secretary has made it a personal priority to improve standards across the board. Strengthening the workforce is central to that goal and there are now a record number of midwives working in the NHS, with over 600 added in the past year.”

articles.title: Justin Trudeau named distinguished fellow at Oxford's Blavatnik School of Government
articles.summary: Former prime minister Justin Trudeau has joined England's Oxford University in a new role.

image.caption: Former prime minister Justin Trudeau is shown on Sept. 11 at the Toronto International Film Festival, where he launched a new production company with Katie Telford, his ex-chief of staff. (Laura Proctor/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada
Former prime minister Justin Trudeau has joined England's Oxford University in a new role.
Former prime minister will become member of school's World Leaders Circle
Trudeau, 54, joined the Blavatnik School of Government as a distinguished fellow and member of the World Leaders Circle, the school said in a news release on Friday.

The release says the former Liberal leader joins an international network of former heads of government, including former New Zealand prime minister Jacinda Ardern and former British prime minister Rishi Sunak.
From 2015 to 2025, Trudeau served as Canada's prime minister before stepping down.
The Blavatnik School, founded in 2010, says it is focused on public policy education and inspiring students to improve the "quality of government and public policy-making worldwide."

items: Freeland believes her resignation led to better outcome for Trudeau, allowing him to exit before likely defeat

blocks.text: Trudeau says in the news release that he is looking forward to "contributing his experience" and working with other leaders to "consider how governments can respond to change and build a more hopeful, inclusive and prosperous future for everyone."
"In the decade that I was prime minister, the world went through profound change both geopolitically and technologically, which fundamentally reshaped our world," Trudeau said.
Ngaire Woods, dean of the Blavatnik School, said Trudeau brings "a wealth of experience, forged through a decade of public service" that will be beneficial to students.
"Our students are the public leaders of tomorrow, and the opportunity to learn directly from those who have navigated the complexities of government ... is invaluable," Woods said in the release.
Trudeau is expected to visit the school later this month.

items: Justin Trudeau launches new film and TV production company

blocks.text: Since stepping back from politics following his resignation as federal Liberal leader and prime minister last year, Trudeau has flitted in and out of the public eye, delivering speeches around the world and popping up at events with his popstar girlfriend Katy Perry.

Last month, Trudeau announced that he was venturing into the entertainment world with the launch of a new media and entertainment production company called Hope & Hard Work, a joint project with Katie Telford, his longtime chief of staff.
With files from CBC News

articles.summary: After a round of blustery fall weather caused ferry cancellations and knocked out power to thousands, B.C. appears set for another blast of wind.

After a round of blustery fall weather caused ferry cancellations and knocked out power to thousands, B.C. appears set for another blast of wind.

On Saturday, Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) issued wind warnings for most of Vancouver Island including Victoria, along with Metro Vancouver, the Southern Gulf Islands, the Sunshine Coast and the Fraser Canyon.
It said another strong low-pressure system is expected to bring powerful southeasterly winds of 70 km/h, gusting up to 90 km/h Saturday afternoon.
ECCC added power outages are possible and warned people to be alert to the potential of falling of flying debris. The winds are forecast to die down towards midnight.
